subsubtopic: GROWTH OF EMPLOYMENT IN ABITIBI-TEMISCAMINGUE AND SAGUENAY-LAC-SAINT-JEAN AREAS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Abitibi- Temiscamingue area was ranked first in Quebec for job creation in 1986. A major economic survey of the progress made by the Quebec labour market in 1986 has brought to light findings which are both unexpected and new. Contrary to what usually happens, the major urban centres such as Montreal and Quebec City did not show as much dynamism last year in the area of employment as such remote regions as Abitibi-Temiscamingue and Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
subsubtopic: GROWTH OF EMPLOYMENT IN ABITIBI-TEMISCAMINGUE AND SAGUENAY-LAC-SAINT-JEAN AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a shameful incident in the record of Canada's treatment of former prisoners of war that needs to be rectified.
Some 22 former Canadian servicemen, including seven Newfoundlanders, one of whom is now deceased, during the Second World War were held as prisoners in a Vichy France prisoner of war camp in Laghouat, Algeria. One of those prisoners, Mr. Jim Templeton of St. John's, was held for a total 472 days.
In 1976 the Parliament of Canada passed the Compensation for Former Prisoners of War Act. Since 1976 these 22 Canadians have been unable to receive from their Government compensation as Canadian prisoners of war. The reasons given are confusing. The Government argues that in order to receive compensation one had to be held by a country engaged in activities against the Allies.
Since the Government and, for that matter, the Allies never formerly declared war on Vichy France, these 22 Canadians, including six Newfoundlanders, have never received adequate compensation. I bring this matter to the attention of my colleagues. It was well exposed on CBC's Sunday Morning this weekend past.
In 1986, Montreal and Quebec City lagged far behind outlying regions as far as job creation was concerned: their growth rates were 1.8 per cent and 1.6 per cent respectively, which are far behind those of 9.2 per cent and 7.3 per cent recorded in Abitibi-Temiscamingue and Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean respectively.
A positive fact is that the unemployment rate has come down in most regions. In the Abitibi-Temiscamingue and the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean areas, the decrease in unemployment has reached 2.3 per cent and 1.5 per cent respectively.
On the other hand, the full-time employment growths have exceeded the Quebec average of 2 per cent, reaching 10.9 per cent and 7.4 per cent in the Abitibi-Temiscamingue and the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean regions respectively.
Mr. Speaker, I am proud of these accomplishments. Thanks to our businessmen, various groups in the economic sector and the efforts of all federal and provincial elected representatives, the working men and women in the Abitibi-Temiscamingue and Lac-Saint-Jean regions will no longer come last in the Province of Quebec.


I hope the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Hees) will move swiftly to ensure that these gentlemen, some of whom died trying to escape that camp, will finally receive justice and the compensation to which they are entitled as Canadians who served their country in very difficult and extreme circumstances.

subsubtopic: GEORGES BANK-EFFECT OF PROPOSED OIL DRILLING PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in late 1986 Texaco announced it wished to drill some test sites within the Canadian section of Georges Bank. In

May 6, 1987
recent weeks this matter has been made more urgent with the announcement by the U.S. Interior Department of a five-year offshore drilling plan for test wells on the American side of Georges Bank.
Georges Bank is a prime fishing area. Atlantic fishermen recognize the potential environmental damage to this sensitive area which can be wrecked by offshore drilling. They are organizing to ensure that this is not allowed to happen. Nova Scotia New Democrats are supporting the fishermen. Bob Levy, our fisheries critic, presented a resolution to the Nova Scotia Legislature on March 31 which reads:
Therefore, be it resolved that this Government state categorically that it will press immediately through its representatives on the Canada-Nova Scotia Offshore Oil and Gas Board for a permanent moratorium on any drilling for oil and gas on Georges Bank and that it will work to have the Georges Bank declared a National Marine Park by Environment Canada as soon as possible to allow for commercial fishing but no offshore drilling.
I call upon the Government of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to proclaim a moratorium on offshore drilling in the Georges Bank area until the feasibility of establishing a National Marine Park is thoroughly studied, and to protest American plans to drill in such a sensitive area. Now is the time for the Canadian Government to act.

subsubtopic: VALUE OF EXPORTS-IMPORTANCE OF FORESTRY TO ALBERTA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, from May 3 to May 9 of this year, we are celebrating National Forestry Week in Canada. Forestry is a vital part of our economic and social life and has enormous impact on our lives as Canadians. Canada is the world's leading exporter of forest products, 22 per cent of the world's total, an incredible $16.2 billion worth of products in 1985.
In Alberta, forestry is an important source of employment. There are 1,200 jobs directly generated by the forest industry in Edmonton alone.
This week I am proud to be able to host the Minister of State for Forestry and Mines (Mr. Merrithew) when he visits the Northern Forestry Centre and the Alberta Forestry Centre. This will be a wonderful opportunity for Edmontonians and Albertans to become more aware of the potential of forestry and its impact on their lives. It is one of the keys to economic diversification in Alberta.
Canada and forestry are synonymous. We all have an obligation to ensure that we protect this natural resource, and that we use it wisely.

Mr. Speaker, victims of the Government's slashing of research and development spending continue to surface long after the dirty deeds are done. The most recent corpses are over 600 students who will find themselves without jobs this summer because of a 25 per cent cut to the budget of the Undergraduate Student Research Awards Program funded by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council.
These awards provided university and industry labs with funds to hire students to do research, to obtain valuable work experience and, hopefully, to go on to graduate study. Everyone except the Government knows that you cannot have more science and technology without people. If we cannot do anything else, we have at least to get young people interested in science.
I call upon the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) to provide funds to NSERC so that it can restore this program to its previous level and provide students with real summer job experience, and get back to providing Canada with the scientific talent that it so desperately needs.

Mr. Speaker, to mark the beginning of Environment Month our Conservative Government supports the initiatives taken by the Fondation quebe-coise en environnement which is sponsoring a wide information and education campaign on the importance of protecting our environment. Ever since it first came into office our Government has always been leading the way in all matters related to environmental protection.
This is why the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Minister of Environment (Mr. McMillan), the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse), the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Cote) and the Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Charest) have assured foundation members that they would make a generous contribution to a special Broadcast entitled "Pour I'avenir du monde, je m'implique", a three-hour environmental presentation to be aired at 6.30 p.m. on May 24 over the Radio-Quebec TV network.
Mr. Speaker, once again our Government has unreservedly endorsed the Environment Month campaign theme, "Pour I'avenir du monde, je m'implique". I urge all Quebecers, particularly my constituents of Chambly, to pay special
May 6, 1987

attention to environmental protection during this National Environment Month.

Mr. Speaker, as one reads the analyses and the recommendations of the World Commission on Environment and Development headed by Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Brundtland one gets the feeling that much of what we do around here amounts to a form of fiddling while Rome burns, or of having the planet disintegrate around us.
I want to make this point because I think that many who are now concerned about the economy should be concerned about the long-term effects of not paying attention to the environment, both in terms of the intrinsic value of the environment as well as the extent to which our economy is based on a healthy environment. We need to abandon the narrow bookkeeping to which all of us are addicted which pits short-term economic deficits against long-term environmental deficits, which may not be able to be repaid and which, in the end, will be profoundly economic deficits as well as environmental ones.
Might I also suggest, more for the benefit of government back-benchers, that we will not be able to solve a great many of these environmental problems if we are committed to allowing the market-place to be the final arbiter of what is done and not done in the name of economic development.

Mr. Speaker, since this is National Business Week, I would like to draw the attention of the House to the performance of the regions, and more particularly the region where the riding of Lotbiniere is located, with respect to job creation in 1986.
In fact, a major study on labour market developments in Quebec tells us that the Mauricie-Bois-Francs region is one of three that have shown remarkable growth in employment. This area ranks third with an employment growth rate of 6.6 per cent. The in increase in full-time jobs La Mauricie-Bois-Francs was 5.1 per cent, 3 per cent above the provincial average.
This progress is the result of the perseverance, active involvement and know-how of the entrepreneurs in this region,
and I think performances like these should be given the attention they deserve.
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to mention more specifically the progress achieved by entrepreneurs in the eastern part of the riding of Lotbiniere, with respect to job creation, and I would urge all those who are active in businesses in my riding to help support this upward trend.

Mr. Speaker, in the two and a half years that this Government has been in power, it has promised the earth and the moon to the people of Greater Montreal. However, despite the Government's catastrophic failure to help Montreal East in the Gulf refinery question, even after three committees, the de Cotret Committee, the Picard Committee and the CREM Committee for Montreal East were set up and three reports were published, the Government has yet to take any action.
The Government of Quebec is still waiting for this Government to locate the space agency in the Montreal area. Second, it expects a real banking centre, not just a night wicket. I would urge the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to wake up and follow through on the commitments made by his Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to the people of Montreal.

Mr. Speaker, on April 26, 1986, I convened a local public conference for residents of my riding of Don Valley East to discuss and learn about the vile types of pornographic material which are so widely distributed and easily available today.
Sergeant Wendy Leaver of Project P of the Metropolitan Toronto Police Force made a thorough presentation depicting violent pornography, much exploiting young children, on video tapes and in magazines.
Almost 100 residents attended this meeting. They were shocked and almost numbed by the devastating, crude and violent scenes depicted. The mood changed to anger when they realized that we have inadequate laws on the books to prevent this type of material from eroding our morals and the very fabric of our society.

May 6, 1987
Oral Questions
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Elnatyshyn) is to be commended for presenting tough new legislation which will make it illegal to import, sell or rent materials defined as pornographic, and illegal to possess child pornography. The basic freedom of expression of Canadians will remain protected by defining a limited class of materials to be prohibited as pornography.
I urge all those who see this Bill as a crude and needless intrusion by public authority into private morals at least to take the time to view and read the sickening material which is available today. If the import and distribution are not curbed through tough legislation, the current material will have a cancerous effect on the future of our society.

subsubtopic: SUPPORT EXPRESSED FOR B.C. TEACHERS' FEDERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to offer congratulations to the B.C. Teachers' Federation and teachers of British Columbia for their fight to improve education in British Columbia.
The B.C. Teachers' Federation has, for almost 70 years, been a vigorous supporter of students, teachers, and education in B.C. It has carried on this fight in recent years against one of the worst provincial Governments in Canada.
The NDP caucus wishes to congratulate and support the B.C. Teachers' Federation and B.C. teachers for their struggle against Bill 20 and Bill 19, two pieces of legislation which destroy the rights of teachers and working people in the Province of British Columbia.

subtopic: SUPPORT URGED FOR MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS RESEARCH CAMPAIGN
SUPPORT URGED FOR MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS RESEARCH CAMPAIGN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, multiple sclerosis is a disease which primarily strikes young people in the prime of life. We have known for over 100 years what the symptoms are and, even though 50,000 Canadians are afflicted with it, we still do not know what causes MS. Recent discoveries by scientists such as Dr. Kenneth Warren, a Canadian, have put us on the verge of finally determining the cause of MS.
As honorary chairperson of the Restigouche Chapter of the Multiple Sclerosis Society, it was my pleasure to participate earlier today with MS officials in presenting a carnation to every Member of this House. The carnation symbolizes the ongoing fight against MS. Despite the significant strides that have been made, the shortage of funds, particularly at this
important stage, has been discouraging to many multiple sclerosis researchers.
I urge the Government and all Canadians to make May, 1987, the best fund raising month on record for MS research so that this insidious and costly disease can be eradicated for all time.

subsubtopic: NEED TO REDUCE GOVERNMENT RED TAPE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Valcourt) has in hand a report dealing with the fact that Government red tape, especially at the federal level, is causing small businesses very serious problems.
Since September 1984, this Government has been making a lot of studies-study after study-and we are still awaiting the Government's policy on the development of small businesses which generate the majority of jobs in Canada.
I suggest Mr. Speaker, the time has come to get out of school, to show where they stand, to show leadership and to assure our Canadian entrepreneurs that the time is right for eliminating or dramatically reducing Government red tape, that is causing serious problems for our Canadian entrepreneurs.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question today must be for the Deputy Prime Minister. While the Prime Minister is touring western Canada, he should be reminded that compared with the start of this decade youth unemployment in western Canada has skyrocketed.
The youth unemployment rate is up 50 per cent in Manitoba compared with 1980. It is up 78 per cent in Saskatchewan. It is up 81 per cent in British Columbia. In Alberta, where the Prime Minister visits today, the youth unemployment rate is up 157 per cent from the start of the decade.
Will the Deputy Prime Minister say now when the Government intends to introduce its national youth strategy which the Prime Minister promised the young people of Canada during the election, or does he really think that photo opportunities in
May 6, 1987

western Canada will be a substitute for finding jobs for young people and the youth of the western Canadian provinces?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is important to point out to the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition that the national unemployment rate has fallen from 11.7 per cent to 9.6 per cent since we have assumed office. The youth unemployment rate at the same time has fallen from 18.3 per cent to 14.8 per cent.
I must remind the right hon. gentleman that unemployment is down in every region of the country. There still are some pockets where there needs to be some substantial improvement, and western Canada is one of them.
Clearly that is an area we are addressing. It will be addressed under western diversification and indeed under the Atlantic Opportunities Program which we will be announcing shortly.

I am very interested to hear that the Deputy Prime Minister feels that Alberta is a pocket. I might say to him that the unemployment rate for young people in Alberta and British Columbia is something about which he and I ought to be jointly more concerned than the reply of the Deputy Prime Minister.

May 6, 1987

subtopic: SCREENING PROCESS-PREPARATION OF LIST OF SAFE THIRD COUNTRIES
SCREENING PROCESS-PREPARATION OF LIST OF SAFE THIRD COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Immigration. The Government has been wimpish in its bilateral dealings with the strong nations of the world. Yesterday it had to show its macho image by beating up on genuine refugees who are nationless. One of the serious flaws with the legislation is the creation of a safe third country list which will determine who can or cannot enter the system.
Why did the Minister establish two pre-screening officers when they do not have discretionary authority to consider claimants coming from a so-called safe third country? In addition, can the Minister inform Canada and this House whether our allies, the United States, which deports both Guatemalans and El Salvadorans, and Great Britain, which deports Tamils, among others, will be on or off such a list?

subtopic: SCREENING PROCESS-PREPARATION OF LIST OF SAFE THIRD COUNTRIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the first step is not a pre-screening. It is a first step to a claimant's right to demonstrate whether he has a personal fear of persecution. There are objective criteria that a claimant has to meet, but there is also another safeguard where, even if there is a shred of evidence that the individual has a fear of persecution, he or she will be directed immediately to step two which is the oral hearing in front of independent members of the refugee determination board.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER DELETE TWO PROVISIONS FROM PROPOSED LEGISLATION
REQUEST THAT MINISTER DELETE TWO PROVISIONS FROM PROPOSED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister knows that the political and diplomatic pressure on Cabinet will be overwhelming. How can the Minister guarantee, as he did last night, that no genuine refugee will be turned away? It is a guarantee that he simply cannot give.
Given that the safe third country list is a dangerous concept and does not recognize new world uprisings, and that prescreening is a barrier to the refugee board, would the Minister agree to scrap these two elements from his legislation and, therefore, allow a refugee claimant to go immediately and directly to the new refugee board? What is the use of having a new system if you cannot get to it?

subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER DELETE TWO PROVISIONS FROM PROPOSED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we must provide a safe haven for those that need one. If the individual already has a legal status in another country, if he has lived there a reasonable length of time and could have sought protection, we will be seeking to ask him to return, assuming that the country has an exemplary record on human rights and assuming the record is excellent in the treatment of refugees of that nationality. As well we will seek advice from credible sources. Our system offers protection to everyone in need.
Let us look at the record of this Government in what we do for the real refugees of the world. We will be bringing 20,000
to Canada this year. That is help to real refugees. If the Hon. Member wants to talk about immigrants, let us boost the immigrant levels, which is what I want to do, and in that component we can have more family members, more independent immigrants, and more refugees.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER DELETE TWO PROVISIONS FROM PROPOSED LEGISLATION

subsubtopic: PRAIRIE POOLS' REQUEST TO MEET PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. The other day, Prairie Pools Inc. sent a telex to the Prime Minister of Canada requesting a formal meeting with the Prime Minister during his western Canadian tour. I spoke to a representative of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool at two o'clock this afternoon and as of then there had been no response from the Prime Minister's Office. Representatives of Prairie Pools had offered to meet the Prime Minister anywhere in any of the three Prairie Provinces. As yet, he is only meeting farmers on one farm and the pools do not have any idea of which farmers he is meeting.
Because of the importance of wheat pools in Canada, will the Deputy Prime Minister return to his office after Question Period, pick up the phone, phone the Prime Minister and ask him to meet with the leaders of Prairie Pools? If he does not do that, he will be content to let the Prime Minister snub the farm leaders of western Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):

He will be meeting with farmers and with the public at a number of public events.

"From agriculture's point of view, the government has been performing rather well in the last six months..." "They gave the deficiency payment; they covered the deficit in the 1985-86 wheat pool accounts without complaint; now the $64-million subsidy-I'm not sure we could ask them to do a whole lot more at this stage."

subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER MEET PRAIRIE POOLS
REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER MEET PRAIRIE POOLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. Yesterday the Prime Minister refused to give a commitment to the request of Mr. Bill Strath, President of Prairie Pools Inc. and representative of 130,000 western grain producers, for a deficiency payment. Now we see the Prime Minister's agenda for his tour of the West does not even include a meeting with Prairie Pools, the largest organization of farm producers on the Prairies.
Why does the Prime Minister's schedule not include any provision for a meeting with this most important group? Why is the Deputy Prime Minister stonewalling on the whole question of a deficiency payment when the West is in such a desperate situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER MEET PRAIRIE POOLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought there was a rule about the repetition of questions. That is the same question that was asked before and I provided an answer.
The fact is that the Prime Minister has met and will meet with representatives of the pools as he will meet with other representatives of farm organizations. A major meeting will be taking place here. The Cairns Group will be meeting and there will be preparatory meetings with the respective farm leaders in regard to that meeting.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to re-inform the House and Canadians that I will be tabling the Government's White Paper on tax reform on Thursday June 18.
Last October in this House I said that tax reform would be based on a number of important guidelines. I set out those guidelines clearly for all Canadians to examine and consider. The White Paper I will be tabling next month has been shaped by those guidelines. It has benefited from the views and insights of the provinces and Canadians across the country.

We said we would make the tax system fairer. We will. We will redistribute the tax burden, so that it will be shared more equitably among taxpayers in similar circumstances.

May 6, 1987
Statements by Ministers

Tax reform will put the Government's revenue sources into better balance, reducing reliance on personal income taxes and increasing the take-home pay of the overwhelming majority of Canadians. It will also provide the Government with a sounder revenue base; not more revenues but more stable and predictable revenues.
Comprehensive tax reform means making improvements in all three parts of the system, personal, corporate and sales tax. Our White Paper will set out specific proposals in each of these areas. To improve the personal income tax system, we will propose lower rates, fewer rates, fewer special preferences and greater use of tax credits rather than exemptions.
Lower rates will benefit the large majority of taxpayers, not just now but well into the future, as their incomes grow and they get to keep more of each additional dollar. Fewer rates will simplify the tax structure. There are now 10 tax brackets. We intend to reduce them to three.
Fewer special breaks for high income earners will reduce opportunities for them to avoid paying their fair share of tax.
Converting personal exemptions and some deductions to tax credits will make the tax system fairer and more progressive. Moving to a system of credits will be a major change, a socially progressive change, a change to the personal income tax system on which future improvements for low income Canadians can be built.
For the corporate income tax system, our proposal is to broaden the tax base by eliminating many special preferences and reducing others. As a result, many more profitable corporations will pay tax, and government revenues from corporate income tax will increase. Broadening the tax base will enable us to lower corporate rates so that they remain competitive with those of our major trading partners and competitors.
Corporate tax reform will support the nation's ability to attract both Canadian and international investment. It will help ensure that business and investment decisions are based primarily on economic merit and growth potential rather than on tax considerations.
The White Paper will also set out proposals to achieve our goal of replacing the federal sales tax system. The current system is flawed and inadequate. We will replace it with a broad-based, multi-stage sales tax.
There are alternative mechanisms to achieving this such as a federal only, multi-stage sales tax, with or without invoices; or a comparable federal-provincial tax with invoices. They vary only in their application and the manner in which they are implemented.
A federal only tax without invoices, which could be called a business transfer tax or a goods and services tax, is relatively simple, both to administer and to comply with, but only if it is
applied uniformly on all goods and services. A federal only value added tax with invoices can be more selectively applied, but would create more compliance and administrative problems in the face of existing provincial retail sales taxes.
A national multi-stage sales tax, in co-operation with the provinces, which could be called the national sales tax, would replace both the federal sales tax and provincial retail sales taxes with a national system. Such an approach offers obvious advantages-a harmonized national tax system, lower administration costs, and less paper burden for businesses. Provincial Governments have indicated some interest in a national sales tax. The concept is clearly worth pursuing.

Mr. Speaker, the government's proposal for comprehensive tax reform aims to give Canada a fairer, simpler tax system, a system that is more effective in encouraging economic activity, jobs and opportunities for Canadians. This is what we are working toward in developing our proposals-proposals that I will table in this House on June 18.

It was only on July 18 that we learned he had changed his mind and would not be tabling this business transfer tax white paper, that he was considering a more comprehensive tax reform which he would unveil in the fall of 1986. Fall 1986 came, nothing happened, except that the Minister announced he would table the white paper at the same time as the 1987 Budget. A few days before the 1987 Budget, on January 30, he told us that he would not table it with the Budget, that it would be put off until spring this year.
Mr. Speaker, I wish I could believe the Minister but he has been crying wolf for so long and announcing tax reforms which never did materialize that this time I am taking a chance when I take him at his word.

Let us hope for the best. We will take the word of the Minister and wait to see what will happen on June 18. We Liberals believe that there has to be a meaningful tax reform package in Canada. We hope that the Minister will deliver on June 18.

Mr. Speaker, June 18 is a memorable day in Europe's history, because it was on June 18 that General de Gaulle
May 6, 1987

called on the French to resist and take up arms against the German forces which had invaded France. I hope that on June 18, the Minister will not be calling on Canadians to pay even more taxes to this Conservative Government.

speechtext:
But not to taxes!

The Minister said in his statement that Canadians could pay less income tax and have, as he suggested, increased take-home pay. But he did not guarantee that Canadians will have more money in their pockets after having paid his new national multi-stage sales tax. The name is so complicated I wonder how we will be able to pay it.
The Minister suggested that he will lower the personal income tax by abolishing preferences. He is saying that we will have fewer special preferences in our personal income tax. I wonder if those preferences that the Minister talked about eliminating will be the first $1,000 of income from interest and dividends, the investment credit for farmers or the flowthrough share deduction for the mining industry. When the Minister says that he will abolish special preferences is he talking about the $1,000 deduction from pension revenue for retired Canadians?

What will happen to the child tax credit and the deduction for child care expenses? Will they be eliminated? Is that the kind of preference to which the Minister was referring in his statement today? The Conservative Government was elected in 1984, and Canadian taxpayers, through their income tax, are paying $22 billion more in 1987 than they were paying in 1984, which represents an additional tax burden of over $1,000 per year and per family, a family with an income of $30,000 and two children, which is not excessive.
Ever since this Government came to power, Canadian taxpayers have been paying considerably more taxes, and when the Minister says he wants to put more justice and equity into the system, is he in fact trying to turn the situation back to what it was before his Government came to power?

Is it the objective of the Government to bring taxpayers back to the point where they were before the Tory Party took office in 1984? The action of this Tory Government has been to tax, retax and surtax Canadian workers and Canadian families in a way that the richer one is, the less tax increases one has had to pay. Is the Minister now telling us that he will correct his own mistakes and bring more fairness to the tax system? We will wait to see how the Minister will achieve that goal and reverse the unfairness that he himself brought into the tax system.

The Minister is proposing to reduce the number of tax brackets to three, from the present 10. I wonder whether three
Statements by Ministers
different tax brackets provide enough room for a progressive personal income tax system. Again, the Minister seems to be indicating that he prefers to protect those on large incomes instead of the average family.
The Minister said he wants to abolish certain tax shelters. He said there will be fewer special breaks for high income earners. Does that mean he will abolish his regressive $500,000 capital gains exemption? Is he going to abolish the flowthrough shares which have been so beneficial to our mining regions? I do not know what he will do. We will have to wait and see how the Minister will achieve that goal and reverse some of the decisions he made in the past.

In another vein, I must tell the Minister that we endorse the idea or approach to replace exemptions by tax credits. However today's statement is not clear enough and we will have to wait and see what happens in that respect.
I would have more remarks to make on corporate taxes, Mr. Speaker, but you are indicating that my time is running short. I should like to comment briefly on the business transfer tax.

I would like to say a few words about the business transfer tax which will now be called the national multi-stage sales tax, the latest tax grab invented by this Government. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is going through the back door rather than the front door, to take billions of dollars from the pockets of all Canadians; the old, the young, and every family. If this multi-stage sales tax is applied as the Minister suggested in his remarks, Canadians may or will have to pay sales tax on food, on haircuts, on everything. I wonder how small businesses will get exemptions. If they do not, it will be a nightmare for them to manage the new taxes.

In short, Mr. Speaker, I would remind the Minister that if he implements his tax reform as he suggests it will have a considerable impact on the provinces. Hopefully his proposals will provide enough firm guarantees for the provinces, particularly those which benefit from equalization payments, to be sure that the tax reform will not reduce their revenues.
I should also remind the Minister that he is committed to simplifying the system. Considering the multi-stage tax he is talking about I really wonder whether the services of lawyers and accountants galore might not be needed to meet the requirements of this new invention of the Mulroney Government, a national multi-stage tax.

speechtext:
The Minister says he can. I welcome his statement that he will table specific proposals on tax reform on June 18. I welcome his renewed commitment to certain principles of tax reform, such as ensuring that profitable corporations pay taxes and eliminating exemptions and deductions in the personal income tax system in favour of tax credits, something which would make the system more progressive. We will have to wait and see whether these words translate into actions.
The Minister himself will acknowledge that he has been far from achieving that standard over the course of the two and half years during which he has been Finance Minister, a period of time during which there has been next to no growth in corporate tax revenues in the exchequer while personal tax revenues have risen by close to 50 per cent. In other words, individual Canadians have been paying for the Minister's deficit reduction strategy and corporations have not had to pay at all. The Minister now says, "Trust me, I am going to make the system fair".
I am particularly concerned, as is my Party, about the latest version of the sales tax which the Minister is announcing. I have been through the various proposals which have been made. We now have the manufacturers' sales tax, the MST. We were going to have a value added tax, a VAT, then it became the business transfer tax, the BTT. The Minister now says that we may have a federal-provincial multi-stage sales tax, an FPMSST. That reminds me of LSMFT. It may be turned into an NST because it will bring in the provincial retail sales tax, the PRST. Anyone who can understand all that understands what the Minister will actually propose.
He is dazzling us with his footwork. I suspect that he may come up with yet another set of proposals in June which will be delegated out for consultation with the provinces, and that it is his intention to back away from changing the sales tax prior to the 1989 election. That may be prudent. It may be caution imposed by his colleagues. However, I have a warning for the Minister with regard to what he is intending to do with this new national sales tax.
The Minister speaks of introducing a broad-based multistage sales tax. He is not clear on whether there will be any
exemptions, but he makes it quite clear that his chosen instrument, the business transfer tax, would have no exemptions at all, that it would be applied uniformly to all goods and services. Is he now proposing that the national sales tax should be applied in the same way? Does that mean that when parents send their children out for daycare, an essential service, they will be paying the Minister's FPMSST on daycare services? Does it mean that a tenant who pays rent and earns a very low income will be paying some kind of federal-provincial sales tax on the service they get in rent? Or does the Minister mean that he still has up his sleeve the intention to have the most essential commodity for survival in life, food, subject to his tax? It is clear that that was the Minister's intention with the business transfer tax.
The Minister is dipping, diving, weaving and bobbing. We do not know exactly what he has to put forward now. However, I want to warn the Minister that if he and his Government intend to try to impose their new national sales tax on food, they will provoke a tax revolt from one end of Canada to the other. New Democrats will be at the front of that tax revolt and we will use everything we can to fight such a measure.

Mr. Speaker, the business transfer tax proposed by the Minister of Finance would have applied to food, the food Canadian families need to survive. Now that the Minister has come up with an alternative, a national sales tax to be imposed in conjunction with the provinces, Mr. Speaker, I ask him: Does the Minister still intend to extend that tax to food as well? If so he is asking for a taxpayers' revolution, a revolution which the New Democratic Party will support, and we will oppose this kind of tax with every means available to us in the House, Mr. Speaker.

The Minister seems to be talking about introducing a duplicate of U.S. tax reform in Canada. There are some good things about that, because there are some elements of the U.S. tax reform which are to be admired, such as the broadening of the corporate tax base, taxing all income equally, and removing wasteful tax preferences. However, there are things we should avoid as well. The Minister should know that Canadians want Canadian tax reform rather than only a clone of what was put into place last year in the United States.
I am particularly concerned that, despite all of the recent evidence which indicates that the Canadian corporate tax system is no more onerous on Canadian companies than are systems in the United States and elsewhere, the Minister talks about a substantial reduction in corporation tax here.

The committee is unanimous that a new law should be built upon a reaffirmation of the public character of broadcasting. The law should also reassert the needs for Canadian ownership and control and, more important, the need to provide a basis for strengthened Canadian programming, while taking into
Petitions
account the distinctive character of French and English language broadcasting.

The House resumed from Tuesday, May 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Andre that Bill C-22, an Act to amend the Patent Act and to provide for certain matters in relation thereto, be read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wish to inform the House that because of the ministerial statement, Government Orders will be extended by 23 minutes.

Mr. Speaker, I have already put on record the opposition to this Bill expressed by the Bishops of the Roman Catholic Church not much more than a week ago, and similarly, the views of the Keystone Agricultural Producers, an organization which represents all the farm commodity groups in Manitoba. The Government's proposal has had almost unanimous opposition from the major newspapers in this country as well. Let me quote from an editorial which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press on March 12, 1987, a newspaper which does not often agree with the views that I and my colleagues in the NDP have expressed. The editorial says in part:
Harvey Andre has tried to write a drug-patenting law designed to balance the consumers' interest in competitively-priced drugs, the drug-innovators' interest in preventing competition and the national interest in expanded medical research, but he has not succeeded.
He has tried to explain to Parliament and to the public reasons why Bill C-22 on patent protection for drug innovations should be adopted and there again he has not succeeded.
Then we have an editorial in The Toronto Star on April 13, 1987, which said:
The amendments have a number of worthwhile objectives:
It says in conclusion:
Once the Bill becomes law, how long will it take before Canada once again has drug prices among the highest in the world?
And who's going to blow the whistle when the multinational drug companies don't live up to their glowing promises but continue to do their research and development in the U.S., Britain and Europe where their head offices are located? A Prices Review Board with no teeth? A federal government with no spine?
Those are very good questions asked by The Toronto Star.
Then we have an editorial in the Kingston Whig-Standard of January 6, which said in part:
Not only are the multinationals on the point of winning, but the Mulroney Government is going to give them far more than its own adviser recommends.
It continues:
-Mr. Andre, who, judging by the way he puts things, appears to care more passionately about the health of Canada's economy.
"As long as people are alive, they're a drain on the health care system," he says-
We certainly do not believe that, Mr. Speaker. The editorial concludes by saying:
It looks as if the government's action will not only make drugs more expensive, it will do nothing to decrease the pushing of unnecessary drugs. In the end, the consumer pays heavily for this sop to a powerful industry.
Then we have the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of January 10, 1987, which says:
The Mulroney government's controversial plan to amend the Patent Act to give the pharmaceutical industry a longer period of protection won't go down any easier with doubting consumers with publication this week of handsome profit statements by the major United States drug manufacturers.
As for the government's assertions that drug costs won't go up in Canada after the act is amended, Canadian consumers will be even less convinced after seeing the profit picture in the American industry and hearing how much their American counterparts pay for medications.
Just a week or so ago the major multinational corporations appeared before a U.S. congressional subcommittee dealing with health matters and were confronted with figures showing that their profits had gone up by more than 20 per cent a year in the last few years. It was pointed out that despite those tremendous profits only about one-third of those profits were channelled into research and development. When we see the head offices of the multinational drug companies acting in that way we should know what to expect from their Canadian subsidiaries.
In a January, 1987, issue of Business Week there was an article entitled "For drug makers, these will be the good old days". The article said:
This should be another record year for the $24 billion pharmaceutical industry ... new products should boost the industry's profits 15 per cent or so beyond last year's 18 per cent increase, to about $5.6 billion. After tax margins could exceed last year's 12.8 per cent.
How much more is the Government prepared to let the multinational corporations rip off the Canadian public? The article then goes into some detail:
Merck's sales could jump to $4.4 billion in 1987, up more than 25 per cent from this year's $3.6 billion, analysts estimate . . . Bristol-Myers-sales this year should jump 15 per cent, to about $325 million.
May 6, 1987

Meanwhile, Eli Lilly & Co. could have a winner in Prozac, an antidepressant already on sale in Belgium. If FDA approval is granted, analysts say, Lilly's 1987 sales could climb by $300 million, to $3.6 billion.
That is what happens. Drugs are developed in the U.S. or Belgium or Switzerland, brought to Canada, and the Canadian consumer pays through the nose. The Globe and Mail had a similar story in January.
The Reuter article was headed "Pharmaceutical companies seen buying shares, raising dividends". It said:
Shareholders could be in line for a bonanza from major pharmaceutical companies which, cash-rich from drug sale profits, are buying back their shares and are considering an increase in dividends, analysts say ... they are sitting on piles of excess cash from their booming business. Some of those funds amount to more than $1 billion (U.S.), which can be a drag on the balance sheet in the current low growth, low interest rate environment.
Industry leader Merck & Co., for example, will have about $1.5 billion in cash at year-end 1986, Bristol-Myers Co. $1.3 billion, Pfizer Inc. $1.4 billion and Eli Lilly & Co. $810 million. Some analysts predict that such cash reserves will double over the next two years.
We are talking about an industry which has already experienced tremendous profits. They do not need this legislation or the encouragement it will give them to make bigger profits, not to invest more in research. As I pointed out earlier in this debate, and in recent months, in the period before 1969, when the present legislation, which the Government is not just amending but is eliminating, was in force, although there were no restrictions on the companies and they had almost unlimited protection of their right to produce drugs which they had researched and developed, there was virtually no research done.
Given the testimony of these companies before the committee that the cost of developing a major new drug from original research to the point where it can be put on the market is in the neighbourhood of $100 million, it is ridiculous and naive to believe that they are going to permit their Canadian subsidiaries to invest that kind of money and effort in Canada to produce a new drug when the market in Canada is so small.
All the evidence indicates that this Bill will increase prices to consumers, and that means to young families with young children, retired people, indeed everyone who uses prescription drugs very frequently. It will substantially increase the profits of drug companies and cost the Canadian public hundreds of millions of dollars. For those reasons we intend to vote against this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday and today the Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) mentioned the objections to Bill C-22 of a Manitoba farm group, Keystone Agricultural Producers. Indeed, in the early fall of 1986 the group issued a news-letter to its members stating their concerns about the Bill in light of their battle to lower the price of farm chemicals.
However, in January this year I attended their annual convention in Winnipeg and discussed the issue with several of their members. After a long discussion they came to the conclusion that if they had legislation like Bill C-22 for farm chemicals they would be ecstatic because their problems would
Patent Act
be solved. I think the House should know what the real story is as far as Keystone Agricultural Producers is concerned.

Mr. Speaker, I have put on the record in the House and in committee the views expressed by Keystone Agricultural Producers as they appear in a letter written to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) on November 25, 1986. It is signed by the president of that organization, Jack Penner.
I have talked to the Secretary of Keystone Agriculture Producers several times. If there had been a substantial change in their views and they had retreated from the position they enunciated very clearly and explicitly in their letter, then I say to the Member for Dauphin-Swan River (Mr. White) that I am sure they would have been in touch with me or the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs or the member, outlining their new position. That has not happened. Therefore, I must assume and I think the member and the Minister have to accept the fact that Keystone Agricultural Producers is still opposed to this, as it was on November 25, 1986.
If the Hon. Member has any real evidence that the official position of Keystone Agricultural Producers has changed, I call on him to put on the record what has happened.
Let me quote from the organization's letter. It is addressed to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, and states:
Dear Mr. Andre:
A recent meeting of the General Council of the Keystone Agricultural Producers Inc., Manitoba's principal general agricultural policy organization, unanimously adopted a resolution calling for our organization to vigorously oppose proposed amendments of the Drug Patents Act, which would allow chemical manufacturing companies patent protection of ten to seventeen years on new pharmaceutical drugs.
The KAP's concerns about the proposed amendments are twofold. Firstly, and most obviously, KAP members share the concerns of those who believe that extended patent protections, will, by limiting the ability of drug manufacturing companies to produce generic copies by means of royalty payments, raise the prices charged to consumers for pharmaceutical drugs to unwarranted levels. Farmers and their families are, of course, part of the general consuming public, and stand to be seriously affected in any such situation.
Secondly, since many of the drug manufacturing companies which produce pharmaceutical drugs are the same companies which produce the chemical formulations used by agricultural producers in the production of primary food commodities, it is our belief that any measures which may be taken with respect to pharmaceutical drugs may have significant implications with respect to the production and pricing of pesticides.
The letter concludes:
Viewed from the perspective outlined above, it is not difficult to understand why an organization such as the KAP would view the amendments you have proposed for the Drug Patents Act as constituting a step in the wrong direction, and we would strongly urge the Government to re-think this ill-advised legislation.
We had a very lengthy and important debate in which more than 100 Members spoke about the problems of western grain producers. Those producers are caught in a situation where they have low prices for the grain they produce while their input costs are increasing. One of those important input costs

May 6, 1987
Patent Act
is fertilizer. It is not surprising that Keystone Agricultural Producers are worried and therefore oppose the Bill. They know that it is not just prescription drugs that will be affected, but farm chemicals and pesticides.
Let me repeat that we are opposed to the Bill. We are joined by organizations such as Keystone Agricultural Producers. I wish the Hon. Member for Dauphin-Swan River would listen to his farm constituents rather than the multinational drug companies, which is what he is doing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Resuming debate.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join the debate on third reading of Bill C-22 today. 1 listened with great interest to what was said yesterday and today.
Quite frankly, I am puzzled by the comment of the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) that the 1969 amendments to the Patent Act which allowed for compulsory licensing increased economic opportunities in the pharmaceutical industry.
I was a member of the Legislative Committee on Bill C-22, as was the Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond. I sat through all but two hours of the 82 hours the committee spent on the Bill and that is certainly not what I heard.
Let me give some examples of what the experts said in the committee. We heard from the Canadian Society for Clinical Investigation which consists of members from across the country. They stated that the amendments in Bill C-22 would protect the fruits of intellectual labour. They went on to say that since 1969, Canada has done very poorly in research and development. In their opinion, Bill C-22 would create the right environment for research and development. In fact, it was that group which made the committee aware that in the past several years advances in psychiatric therapy due to drugs has saved approximately $1 billion a year in hospital care.
We heard from the National Biotechnology Advisory Committee which called the present law a disincentive in the investment climate.
We heard from Doctor Chretien of the Montreal Clinical Research Institute who said that chemists who work for an innovative drug company do not get the same protection as, for example, a scientist who may work for Dupont Corporation who develops a new polymer. He said that pharmaceutical scientists are discriminated against because of the present legislation.
We heard from Doctor Manson, who represents Biomega, a Canadian biotechnology company. According to him, the system is not providing protection to domestic biological companies. He stated that this is a major growth area in human natural products, immunology and diagnostics and that our present system is not providing protection for that industry.
It is also important to note that amendments brought forward by the Government at committee stage have answered many concerns and questions raised by Doctor Manson and others representing Canadian biotechnology companies.
We heard from Doctor Spiro of the University of Toronto, representing the Coalition of Scientists. In his estimation, Bill C-22 will increase both basic and clinical research. The 1969 Bill had a bad affect on medical research, according to Dr. Spiro.
We heard from Dr. Jacques Gagne, a pharmacist-* pharmacologist and Dean of the University of Montreal. He was a little more emphatic. He said the 1969 amendments were the worst thing that ever happened to research in pharmacy in Canada. He calls Bill C-22 a major step in the right direction.
We heard also from a Mr. Ian Thompson. He is not an expert or scientist. He has two children with cystic fibrosis. He said the future of his family depends on research and new and better drugs. Who is doing the research in drug therapy? It is certainly not the generic companies. Dr. Chretien, whom I mentioned earlier, said generic companies do zero per cent in research. Their motive is profit only. As Mr. Thompson said, the future of his family depends on research, and therefore, depends on the innovative drug firms.
The Medical Research Council of Canada did not appear before the committee, but I have its report dated February 1987 from which I would like to quote very briefly:
After the Patent Act was amended in 1969 to provide for compulsory licensing to import, the growth rate of innovative pharmaceutical companies' R and D investment in Canada is said to have declined.
This decline in growth rate has been more than twice as severe as that for the industry worldwide and also about twice as severe as for other industries in Canada.
The report continues:
The direction which the patent legislation will take if and when the new Act is passed cannot but be favourable to the expansion of medical research in Canada.
The Hon. Member from Cape Breton-East Richmond read a letter yesterday from the Manitoba Women's Institute saying that we were accusing opposition Parties of promoting fear. In quoting from this letter, the Hon. Member stated that the Women's Institute was certainly not promoting fear. I agree, it is not promoting fear but is the victim of this campaign of misinformation. We have the misfortune in Manitoba, I must say, of having a New Democratic Provincial Government and we have been bombarded with misinformation.
I would just very briefly like to list some of the facets of Bill C-22 which should be remembered because I think it ties in with my following remarks. Under Bill C-22 all generic products sold today will continue to be sold. New generic products may be marketed as early as seven years after a brand product is approved for marketing. Today on average it takes nine and a half years for such a process. Why is that? I
May 6, 1987

mentioned a few moments ago that the only motive of the generic drug firms is profit. They do zero research according to some of the top minds in the industry in Canada.
Generic companies are now seeking licences for more than 40 products. Under Bill C-22 every single one of these products can be marketed within the next five years. A very important aspect of Bill C-22 as well is the establishment of the Drug Prices Review Board. Under the Drug Prices Review Board, the prices of all patent drugs will be reviewed annually. The prices of all new products will be compared to the prices of the products with which they compete to ensure consistency with the established market prices. The board as well will have the power to roll back prices if the innovative firms are not keeping their commitments to research and development.
The board will measure annually the impact of the activities on drug prices and these reports will be made public. These aspects are quite clear. The fact that Dr. Eastman will head up the committee and, in his own words, he feels the committee will be beneficial and effective, makes me think that the process will work very well.
The innovative firms at the same time have promised to expand R and D from 4.9 per cent to 8 per cent by 1990 and to 10 per cent by 1995. I have a long list of examples of innovative firms which have pledged millions of dollars, over $800 million, in increased R and D and capital spending.
I would also like to mention briefly, before 1 get into the Opposition tactics, some indisputable facts about the pharmaceutical industry.
I am a licenced pharmacist in the Province of Manitoba. There are over 5,000 drugs on the market in Canada at the present time. I can pick at random 100 of those products off my shelves in my drug store, and 93 at the present time will have no generic competition. Seven per cent is all that have generic competition at this time. What does that tell us? It tells us that only 7 per cent of the drugs on the market in Canada right now are financially attractive to the generic companies. The other 93 per cent, although they are saving lives across the country, are not rich enough to attract the generic companies. The generic companies are not doing the research. They are copying 7 per cent of the drugs for the sake of pure motive and we are losing our scientists because of it.
I attended a press conference in Winnipeg late last fall which was set up and held by several experts in the field. There were scientists from the University of Manitoba and St. Bonifice Hospital Health Sciences Centre. We heard from research scientists from the Children's Hospital in Winnipeg that two new products had been developed by a scientist who packed his bags and moved to Europe to further develop those drugs because of the present compulsory licensing laws in Canada.
I should also note at this time that we expect, upon passage of Bill C-22, $50 million of increased research and development spending in my home Province of Manitoba.
Patent Act
In light of these facts, what has the New Democratic Party been saying, particularly in Manitoba? For purely political reasons it is preying upon the fears of the sick and elderly. In fact that Party is not just preying on those fears; in my opinion it is creating false fears. I believe it is quite understandable that Canadians have questions about new legislation for any federal Government. However, the misinformation being spread by the New Democratic Party of Manitoba and across the country is reprehensible. It is creating totally false fears in the minds of the very people it pretends to protect. I would like to go through a few examples to prove my point.
My home town, Swan River, Manitoba, is a small town. The local Member of the Legislature from that area is a Cabinet Minister in the NDP Government of Manitoba. He sent a letter to the editor late last fall and I would like to read a few lines because it emphasizes the campaign of misinformation being perpetrated in Manitoba. I quote from a Minister of the Crown in Manitoba:
Dear Sir:
I wanted to express my concern about Ottawa's intention to ban generic drugs. A federal Bill to prohibit the sale of "generic" drugs-is expected to be introduced during the current session of the Canadian House of Commons.
He continues in his letter to urge that Canadians should write to the Prime Minister. For him to say that generic drugs will be prohibited is ridiculous. It is absolute nonsense. That letter was written by a Minister of the Crown in Manitoba who should be believable.
At the same time I have a letter which was sent out to most Manitobans from New Democratic Members of the legislature from across the province. I have several in my possession and they are word for word; the only difference is the signature. Although the letter does not speak in quite as profound terms as the previous letter, the first line talks about the prospect of higher prices, something that is worrying a lot of people these days. My contention is that worry is being spawned by the New Democratic Party. The letter says that drug prices will increase significantly, and for a full page the letter goes on to create fear in the minds of the elderly, which is shameful. Those are the very people that that Party professes to protect.
As recently as this week, the Hon. Member for Yorkton- Melville (Mr. Nystrom), while introducing a petition, bootlegged in some editorial comment on Bill C-22. He said that Bill C-22 would hurt the Saskatchewan Drug Plan and smiled when he said it as though that was quite funny. It is interesting that during the hearings of the Legislative Committee on Bill C-22 we heard from the Deputy Minister of the Saskatchewan Health Department and the Executive Director of the Saskatchewan Prescription Drug Plan. I would like to quote from the testimony of Mr. Walter Podiluk, the deputy Minister of Saskatchewan Health Department:
We present to you the Saskatchewan position, based on our experiences with a drug plan which is the most comprehensive and the most universal of any in Canada ... At the present time, after some fairly careful examination of the provisions and the features of Bill C-22, we feel it has the potential to control the inflationary spiral of pharmaceutical costs. We feel it also has the potential to create a more stable investment climate and stimulate employment.

May 6, 1987
Patent Act
Because Saskatchewan recognizes the potential good that can be derived from
the Bill, we are prepared to accept the principles and the thrust behind it.
That was from representatives of the Saskatchewan Prescription Drug Plan.
Finally, I wish to refer to one last letter which is the second in a series of letters. It was sent to thousands of Canadians last week or the week before last. It is from the Leader of the New Democratic Party and is dated April 13, 1987. It is a follow-up to a letter sent out on September 30. The letter reads in part:
Dear Friend,
You and your family could soon be paying a small fortune for prescription
drugs, just so that big foreign-owned drug companies can increase their profits.
Further in the letter he states that Bill C-22 would mean that:
-all new drugs coming onto the market will be as expensive as the drug
companies wish to make them-for 10 years.
That sentence ignores the Drug Prices Review Board which will control the price of all drugs, not just those 7 per cent from drug companies which are rich enough to attract the generics at this time. Further on in the letter he mentions a monopoly for drug companies. Patent experts who appeared before the committee told us that this situation is not a monopoly situation because these products, if not for the innovative firms, would not be in existence in the first place and there would be nothing to copy.
Further on in the letter the Leader of the NDP states that generic drugs save Canadians more than $211 million per year. He does not mention that under Bill C-22 it has been estimated, using the same criteria as that used by Dr. Eastman, that consumers would save not $211 million but anywhere from $226 million to $366 million. He fails to mention that fact.
The best part of the letter is found in the last couple of paragraphs. Beside a political gain I was wondering what the Leader of the NDP had in mind when he sent this letter. He
states:
Make a contribution to the New Democrats' campaign for fair drug prices.
Members of the New Democratic Party are using these false fears not just for political gain but as a fund-raising campaign. That is something which is unheard of and totally shameful, in my opinion.
1 feel that my contention that Canadians have been misinformed by the NDP is proven by this letter. That includes the Keystone Agricultural Producers about whom the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) was speaking just a short while ago. They were misinformed and have sent out a newsletter advising their members to oppose Bill C-22. In my discussions with members of Keystone Agricultural Producers, as well as the President, I found they have softened that view and are now saying that if they had such a system in effect for farm chemicals they would be far better off.
This nonsense that is being spread-and I think spread is a good word because coming from a farming community in
Manitoba we spread much of what is being spread by the NDP here-is creating false fears. It is certainly not helping the debate on Bill C-22.
In the opinion of the Canadian Medical Association which represents almost 44,000 doctors Bill C-22 is good for Canada and good for the health care system. Rather than seeing Bill C-22 as a curse, the generic companies should see it as a chance to become involved themselves in research and development and invest their profits. Their profits are well up there. They should invest those profits in the pharmaceutical industry and in pharmaceutical technology. Let us not forget that if a generic company makes a major discovery in pharmaceutical technology, that discovery would be protected for between seven and ten years just as any discovery of an innovative firm would be protected for the same length of time. As a nation we must protect intellectual property rights.
I was in a conversation last fall with a gentleman who phoned me up at home one evening to talk about Bill C-22 and his opposition to it. It so happens that at the present time this same gentleman is writing a book which he hopes to have published in the next couple of months in hard cover. I said to him: "Well, sir, what if the day after you have this book published in hard cover selling for $20, $30, $40, someone down the street publishes the same book in paperback and sells it for $3.95? Would that not be the same as Bill C-22?" I think that is a very apt analogy. It got him thinking twice about Bill C-22 and his opposition to it.
The Canadian Pharmaceutical Association, of which I am a member, publishes a journal monthly. In the October, 1986, edition there is an editorial on the Patent Act changes that we are debating today. It is entitled "A Needed Reform". The article states that the Canadian Pharmaceutical Association has taken a definite stand on the proposed patent reforms. The association supports them because it believes that the amendments will improve the quality of the Canadian pharmaceutical industry and ultimately benefit consumers. I share this optimism, the optimism of my colleagues across Canada, in the belief that increased research development will occur under Bill C-22 and will result ultimately in a superior health care system for all Canadians. The four-year review that is built into Bill C-22 will ensure that the innovative drug companies are keeping up their end of the bargain.
I would like to close with a short verse that I read many years ago and happened to come across just a few days ago. It reads:
For the want of a prescription, a sale was lost For the want of a sale, a profit was lost
For the want of a profit, an investment was lost
For the want of an investment, a research project was lost
For the want of a research project, a new drug was lost For the want of a new drug, a patient was lost
Innovative drugs help support today's research and tomorrow's breakthroughs which are good for Canada. I urge the House to support Bill C-22.
May 6, 1987

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have the honour to inform the House that a message has been received from the Senate informing this House that the Senate has passed, without amendment, Bill S-6, an Act to amend the Food and Drugs Act.
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Andre that Bill C-22, an Act to amend the Patent Act and to provide for certain matters in relation thereto, be read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on third reading of Bill C-22.
Mr. Speaker, it is both sad and unfortunate that the Conservative Government has failed to consider the recommendations made by the Official Opposition, by my colleague from Saint-Michel-Ahuntsic (Mrs. Killens) and my colleague from Cape Breton, who both worked very hard to ensure that this Bill, whose purpose is ... I think it is important to recall for the benefit of the people watching us, that before 1969, it was the law of the jungle as far as the price of prescription drugs was concerned.
Because there was no competition at the time, and companies doing research enjoyed considerable protection in the form of patents, when their research was successful, on for instance a new drug to alleviate pain, the companies could arbitrarily set a price of $5, $10, $15 or $20 on their products. For 17 years, they held a monopoly, and people who needed this drug to alleviate pain were at the mercy of those who took advantage of the situation at the time, and thought only in terms of profits.
Faced with this situation and this attitude, in 1969 the Liberal Government decided to protect the Canadian consumer, while the Hon. Member who spoke earlier, the Conservative Member, his only concern was the company and research, never mind the price to be paid by the consumer and by the sick who need prescription drugs to alleviate pain or cure their illnesses. Faced with such abuses on the part of the multinationals the previous Government decided to eliminate this patent protection, with the result that the health product market became more competitive. The same medication, the same pill produced the same effects but it did not have the same appearance. Still the person who needed this medication to relieve suffering or cure such and such disease did not have to pay so much.
Patent Act
The Eastman report pointed out that Canadian consumers saved $211 million in 1983. When we say consumers, we have to keep in mind that we are referring to people whose condition is not normal and who need drugs because they are sick.
Even so, with the passage of time and perhaps rightfully so because of the lesson the multinationals drew from having to compete, the Liberal Government agreed to review the situation and appointed the Eastman Commission to find out whether after a few years we ought to maintain the same process and give no protection to companies which carry out research, or whether it is true that research can indeed be very costly and there ought to be a minimum of protection. Instead of giving up under pressure and yielding to blackmail from the multinationals or anybody else, the Government appointed an inquiry commission. After consultations Commissioner Eastman recommended that consumers who are sick need to be protected, this was the first and most important consideration, but at the same time he advocated a certain degree of intellectual protection for companies doing research so as to protect and maintain employment levels in research in Canada and Quebec. The Eastman Commission recommended a four-year protection.
But here again unfortunately-always in keeping with the Conservative approach so perfectly described by the Conservative Member who spoke before me-the poor company was losing a bit of money, it needed help, no matter what. Sick people will have to pay more, but to him it is a minor consideration, it does not really matter.
This legislation and the attitude show the position and attitude of the three national parties. The legislation shows that clearly. In the legislation you have protection-someone, a Prime Minister who is kneeling before the drug multinational corporations, as he knelt before the banking institutions, as he knelt before the Americans. And the drug multinational corporations told him: "Listen, you give us this, and what we need is 10 years without any market competition. Let consumers pay more, that is of minor interest". They said: "We will put up money", but that is taxpayers' money, federal money, $100 million to compensate the provinces, because they are footing the bill for the drugs used by people on Quebec welfare, by hospital patients and others.
Let us not forget how little this Tory Government shies away from getting money on the backs of patients. We remember the 10 percent tax on drugs-hard-nosed as it is, it will not stop at that. This is the second time it is using sickness in Canada-the first time to reduce the Canadian Government deficit that covers the Prime Minister's luxury travels, and now to enrich the multinational corporations.
But you have at the other end the New Democratic Party, and the Hon. Member who just spoke clearly showed that the NDP's intellectual honesty is not Canada's best. As McEnroe would say, it is no great shakes.

May 6, 1987
Patent Act
So you have clear, specific proof. The NDP opposes any change. And this shows that the NDP does not understand Quebecers at all. And this is where the NDP clearly shows that in spite the fine promises and the fine faces made by the NDP Leader in Montreal, as soon as he gets back to Ottawa, as soon as he crosses the river, he does not even remember what a Quebecer is and what he is asking for.
He does not even know. Some people. There is nobody in the NDP, not even the turncoat for Terrebonne who left the Progressive Conservatives, who transfered in the meantime- he took a seat anywhere, and he landed beside the NDP, because the Rhinoceros Party and the Liberal would not have him. Even he, who is from Quebec, did not dare rise to represent the interests of Quebecers.
And for once in Quebec, you know that in Quebec, the Liberals and the Pequistes are hard-headed. The Parti Civique and the RCN find it hard to agree on anything. They are often bickering, but on the matter of drug patents, dating back from the time when the PQ was in Government and the Provincial Liberals in Opposition, there was a unanimous vote in the National Assembly to urge the federal Government to grant a minimum of patent protection to keep Quebec brains in the Montreal area, to give a certain credibility, honesty that is due to multinationals, but not to do like the Conservatives who bow to blackmail and give everything to the multinationals.
Again, the NDP is unaware of what took place in Quebec. Personally, last year, I took part in the Montreal economic summit, which drew together people of all political stripes: representatives from the Quebec Government and Opposition, and Members of the Liberal, PQ and Conservative parties. Personally, I was there for the Liberal Party at the federal level. There was no NDP representative. There were people from the RCM and Civic parties. The Civic Party was then in power in Montreal. There were union representatives from the CSN. I suppose the NDP does not know about the CSN, for it operates only in Quebec. It is all Chinese to them. The CSD is another union which operates in Quebec. I can understand that the NDP leader would not know about the CSD; although he pays a lightning visit to Montreal once in a while, he does not know about the CSD.
But there were also representatives from the FTQ, which is a member of the Canada Labour Congress. Personally, I am a paying member in good standing of the FTQ. There was also a guy named "Ti-Louis" Laberge who is not afraid to speak out and who is neither a Liberal, nor a PQ nor a Conservative. He was sitting with the others around the table and all of them were on the same wave-length. They were asking that the federal Government introduce a bill providing a minimum of protection for patents. It is a well known fact that the drug manufacturers are concentrated in the greater Montreal region. There are a few in Quebec City and some more in other regions. We have to protect and keep our scientists.
Again, I should like to remind the House that it was not "Ti-Louis" Laberge who stated, even if at one time he did negotiate with the Premier: Just a minute, the multinationals
and you are bedfellows; you are giving them all they want. Now, this is a different matter.
Again, this panel included Golden Agers. These people too were unanimous. Then, all of a sudden, the NDP comes along and says: Let's keep things as they are. Let us maintain the status quo. We keep the status quo, Quebecers are not so important. We do not care about Quebecers. Such is the attitude and the behaviour of the NDP with respect to the fair and just claims of the Quebec people. The NDP, and the Leader of the NDP when he wants to defend the automobile industry in his constituency, in his province, often tries to get the support of Quebecers, and he would like them to understand the problems of other regions. But when they try to have the NDP understand their specific needs, because in all their speeches they say that they recognize the specificity of Quebec, when they are asked to say in specific terms how we should go about it, the NDP demonstrates that it is not this or that, that it is not the right way.
Let me go back to the attitude of the present Government. It is unfortunate that the suggestions, the amendments put forward by my colleague the Hon. Member for Cape Breton- East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) were not accepted.
