He was expressing the fair, just and logical views of the majority of the Canadian people who were asking for a basic principle. I believe that all Members of the House of Commons who represent their constituencies, who represent the Canadian people, know very well that the least organized people in Canada are the sick, that there is no association for them to get together and lobby the governements, and tell them: Hold it, you are hurting us! Those people suffer. They do not have time to get organized. The first duty of every Member of the House of Commons should be to defend the interests of those who are least able to defend themselves. And it should have been the role of Conservative Members to tell the Government and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney): Hold it, Canada is not run by multinationals. Let us reject their blackmail when they say: If you do not give us that Bill with 10 years, we will not make as many investments. If the Prime Minister had shown that he had guts, that he could hold his own, he would have said: Hold it, man, you will take what we will give you. We have been elected by our fellow citizens to defend the interests of the Canadian people from sea to sea, not to be blackmailed by multinationals.
He could have said that a commission, an inquiry carried out with public funds, had enabled experts to say that four years would provide adequate protection for consumers in terms of drug prices. With four years, there would be protection for research and academics who want to work in that field, and the multinationals would continue to make a profit, even without a ten-year monopoly. After all, they did not go bankrupt. Now listen, the multinationals are not in business to please you or me. They do research because they think there is money in it, otherwise they would not bother.
May 6, 1987

Unfortunately, concessions have been the order of the day. As for the NDP Members, initially they had set up their petitions opposing the measure but felt they could not send their petitions to Quebec. Maybe there was a bit of hypocrisy in this, because they knew perfectly well they would be getting into a hornet's nest. However, I felt they might have realized at some point that if they want to get candidates elected in Quebec, they would have to show a minimum of respect. They should go to Quebecers and ask what their position is. They should ask the PQ and the people who defend the interests of Quebecers from the Montreal area in the National Assembly what kind of distinctions they make. They may be right and they may be wrong. But they did not do that. They tried to cover up the problem so that they ended up defending their own ideological interests but not the interests of Canadians, and especially not the interests of Quebecers. Recently, questions were asked in the various regions, both in the National Assembly and elsewhere, and' both parties were always asking the federal Government to proceed quickly. However, I repeat that this is not reflected in the Bill we are being asked to adopt today on third reading, Bill C-22, which unfortunately will have the effect of considerably increasing the price of prescription drugs in the future.
Some Conservative Members will say: The provinces will foot the bill. But from whom are the provinces getting the money? From the taxpayers. Consumers will be paying more taxes to cover the cost to provincial plans of higher priced drugs.
Other Convervative Members suggested: "No, there is no serious problem there, they have private insurance". Well, who is paying for private insurance covering the cost of drugs, the Blue Cross or someone else. The consumers again. The fact is that prices will increase, insurance companies will raise their premiums, insurance companies operate on the basis of a 10 per cent profit on cost, well, they too will be looking for extra profits. But who will be footing the bill? Again, consumers.
And Conservative Members once more forgot about senior citizens. Yes, seniors again. It may be in an underhanded way the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) who announced today that on June 18, he will be introducing the tax reform ... Is he going to mislead senior citizens as he once did concerning the de-indexing of old age security? Will Mrs. Solange Denis have to stay at the door to watch for our national "Charlie Brown"?
But they forgot there are four million people in Canada who will have to dig into their pockets. And they are not rich people, but people working at the minimum wage in convenience stores, people who work week-ends. Four million people who may not transfer the cost of drugs to their Provincial Government because they are not on welfare, because they have an income, they work. That includes equal numbers of young people, older ones and seniors.
There are four million people who have no more protection, who do not have Blue Cross, who do not earn enough to pay for the protection of private insurance. On top of that they have to try, out of their meagre earnings, to put as best they can some money aside in case they have to buy drugs if one of their kids gets sick.
Patent Act
And here, with the 10 year protection, we will come back to that, that during 10 years .. . Ah, at the start, during the first year, the multinationals will be kind, they will report, they will say: We are planning a one cent increase. Look how nice we are. Three, four or five years later, when we are not looking anymore, they will go ahead, they will go all out. Hey? After six years they will say: Just in case they change anything we should do like the Conservative MPs, let us grab everything we can before we get beaten.
Why did the Conservative Government not choose to negotiate just like the Eastman Commission would have done? Eastman recommends four years, the companies are trying for 10, so let us settle the matter and call it five years. You have only five years. After five years-Mr. Speaker, I see I have only one minute left-after five years we will review the legislation to see whether it should be maintained. No, Sir, it is the other way around. This is just another way of speaking, we let them buy us off, not for very much because we are not worth very much these days. So we tell the multinationals: You have 10 years. We give them 10 years and then set up a supercommittee to investigate. Imagine, we are not even sure whether research will be done in Germany .. . Imagine how much we will have to pay for this committee which will go traipsing around the world to make an inquiry into a handful of powder .. . Who studied that? Make an investigation. We will have Sherlock Holmes-type investigators coming out of the woodwork. It will cost a fortune and we will be no better off.
After five years the committee will report: Well, maybe we should make some changes. So the multinationals will say: Just a minute, you passed a law, we have 10 years, it was up to you to think about it. Today's Conservative Members will no longer be here in five years, they will all be out, but the people will be left with the problem created by the Conservative Members.
I see some of the Conservative Members are laughing. It is very funny. I can appreciate that some of them may have an interest in this. Perhaps they are shareholders of the multinationals. Personally I am clean, I have no shares in the multinationals. I can understand that a shareholder would be interested and anxious to see the Bill passed, he will be here day and night, hopefully the shares will go up and he will make a bundle. But that is not my interest nor my intention, Mr. Speaker.
We are talking about our constituents. The Conservative Members who are here ought to keep in mind that maybe tomorrow somebody in the family will be sick. You are laughing now, but maybe one of your relatives will take sick tomorrow and you will say that the high cost of drugs is scandalous. How did it happen? People will tell you that you should have been on your toes when you were there. You should not have given in to blackmail from the multinationals. You should not have let them buy you off. It is your responsibility to think about the welfare of Canadian taxpayers first instead of your own.

May 6, 1987
Patent Act
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I do not know if there is still hope, for the Bill has reached third reading. 1 am under the impression that Conservative Members have cash registers instead of hearts. There is nothing that can be done about that. But I am still hoping, one never knows . . . Since the Bill will be referred to the Senate, maybe it will be returned here with amendments that will enlighten Conservative Members, and I trust that the NDP Members will remember how unfair and offensive to Quebecers they have been in this debate.

Mr. Speaker, I wish first of all to congratulate the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) for his eloquent speech in favour of the neediest Canadians. I do not think the House has a better defender of the needy than the Hon. Member from Montreal-Sainte-Marie. Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member mentioned a category of citizens who will undoubtedly be the most affected by the change proposed by the Government. This category of some 4 million people do not necessarily live on welfare, are not necessarily wage-earners and are not eligible because of their job to medical assistance programs which would provide them with free drugs and they will be faced with prohibitive costs when purchasing medicine.
These Canadian men and women just cannot afford such a burden. But in spite of all this, I think that demonstration of the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie is quite eloquent and shows that there will be cruel and severe consequences for a great many men and women. Still, the Government tries to justify its odious drug legislation by saying that it will create new jobs. I know that the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie represents a riding in the eastern part of Montreal Island, in Quebec, which is severely affected by high unemployment.
Could the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie indicate to the House whether he sees any benefit or positive results for the Island of Montreal as far as job creation is concerned, following the adoption of this Bill which is cruel indeed to Canadian men and women?

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif) for his very important question. The Conservative Government would have us believe that it introduced this legislation, which provides a 10-year protection period, in order to create jobs. The problem is that we cannot be sure that the Bill in its present form will create jobs in Quebec. These jobs are not a sure thing. There may be a couple of jobs in the construction industry since it seems another building is going up. Sure. Suppose they need a carpenter. Today, a carpenter doesn't have that much to do on a construction site. It is mostly iron and steel and concrete. However as far as scientific research and the real brains are concerned, there is absolutely no guarantee.
Knowing the Conservatives, are they going to oblige a company to create jobs in Canada? We saw what happened with Gulf-Ultramar. The Government decided to allow the
sale of the Gulf refinery to a foreign company, which then decided to close down the refinery. The jobs were lost. We saw this in the decision regarding Dome Petroleum and Amoco. The Hon. Member is right to be concerned because this Bill means the consumer will have to pay more. According to the Conservatives, this will create more jobs in research, but there is nothing to guarantee and nothing proves that the jobs in research will go to Canada and Quebec. I wouldn't be surprised, in fact, I am sure that the people of Quebec fully expect to be shafted once again, as they were so many times before. They will have to foot the bill but will have nothing to show for it, as we saw in the case of the General Motors plant in Sainte Therese.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I want to make a comment, then I will have a question for my colleague from Montreal-Sainte-Marie who poses as the champion of the elderly. He usually does a very good job, but still there is a limit to wanting to protect the poor, the orphan, and the elderly. Demagogy comes easy in this field, and I think my colleague has earned his spurs in that respect. Mr. Manuel Maitre, the director or president of the Quebec Federation of Senior Citizens, had this to say when he appeared before the committee, and I quote: It often happens that the senior citizens or groups of senior citizens-because politicians tell them this-say that they are going to pay more if this legislation is adopted.
Mr. Maitre said: This is a total falsehood because in Quebec there are presently 4,100 pharmaceutical products for which they can get a refund. Five years ago there were 1,400 in Ontario and 800 in Saskatchewan. Mr. Maitre went on to say: What you have there is a complete arsenal, you can poison the whole planet with it. And one of the recommendations of the Quebec Federation of Senior Citizens is to urge the Government to legislate in an attempt to cut down the use of medicated drugs. Physicians are so handy with their prescription pad that senior citizens become sick.
So the only drugs they need now are covered. Well, how can you justify your position when we know that this group of sick and elderly people are covered by health insurance plans?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say to the Hon. Member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mrs. Bertrand) that before, on the matter of the de-indexing old age security pensions, she stated clearly and publicly that a Government was under no obligation to honour its promises, its commitments.
And she just showed clearly, and I mentioned earlier in my speech, that indeed the NDP does not understand the Quebec Federation of Senior Citizens, who ask for minimum protection. But the aim, what the Hon. Member is asking, is this: Do senior citizens over-use drugs? Physicians and studies suggest they do. But it is not by granting patent protection that the over-use situation will be corrected. Senior citizens will not change on the matter of aspirin if they use too much.
May 6, 1987

It is therefore my view that the Hon. Member for Brome- Missisquoi took the wrong road to reach her goal. If education is needed to urge people to use less and less drugs, it is not by keeping money with the multinationals that this will be accomplished. The Government could have taken money and put it into education, prevention through the CLSC, the senior citizens' clubs, and I would be highly supportive of such a move.
But what we now have before us is strictly a case of someone kneeling before the multinationals, someone wanting to give extra money to the multinationals. This holds nothing good for consumers as a whole. And above all, it will not protect patients because there are drugs patients have to use to alleviate their pain.
I would therefore urge the Hon. Member, knowing her sense of responsibility, to tell her Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) that in order to achieve her goals, in order to prevent people from using drugs unnecessarily, other methods and other steps could be taken. I would be ready to co-operate. But let them reduce the bill, let them provide for a five-year protection and a review of that protection five years down the road. But first, we must protect consumers. And if the Government really wants to save jobs, help our brains, our scientists, our learned people, well, it is not by slashing research funding and so on that this will be accomplished. It is not by simply asking patients to become increasingly ill that jobs will be created for people with brains. Because the Government attitude is getting stupid there.
Mr. Speaker, I think there are three things to consider. If Conservative Members want our scientists and researchers in whatever field to have jobs, well, instead of spending money on the banks and handing out capital gains tax exemptions, instead of letting the Prime Minister transfer a penitentiary to his own riding, instead of all this foolishness, let them take the money and manage it properly, and provide funding for research and create jobs for people and protect the sick. Now, if she wants a program to educate people to be less dependent on prescription drugs, I think that is a very good idea. So let's provide the funding and do whatever is necessary to achieve that goal.
[DOT] (noo)

Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to rise today in strong support of Bill C-22. As we are quickly coming to a close of this debate, perhaps we should review a little of the history over the past few months. There has been much talk about there not being enough time to debate Bill C-22. Canadians have seen what has happened. We have had days and days when members of the opposition Parties rose and said, "I move that so and so be heard". On one day we voted every half an hour. That is not responsible opposition. It is time members of the Opposition learned that they are here to oppose Bills that are bad but not to oppose every Bill that comes before the House.
Patent Act
This Bill was introduced on November 6, read for the first time on November 7, and debated at second reading stage on November 20, 21, 24, 25 and December 5. From there, the Bill went into committee and that committee sat every day of the week beginning December 8 and going right through until March 5. There was adequate time for members to look into the Bill.
From speaking to some of my colleagues in the Liberal Party, I have learned that they do not believe that there is very much wrong with this Bill. As a matter of fact, looking back in history, this Bill was introduced in the Thirty-second Parliament by the former Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, but it was botched up and the Government did not get it through. Now we will vote on this Bill and I urge all members to support it because it is a good one.
I think we should look at the Bill itself. It talks about the protection of intellectual property. Intellectual property is a very important thing. People talk about generic companies not being able to work alongside innovative companies. Generic companies presently produce 7 per cent to 8 per cent of all the pharmaceuticals in Canada. In the United States where there is 17-year patent protection legislation, generics have grown to 25 per cent of the market. I see in the future a generic industry and an innovative industry working side by side in Canada. We have to remember that the last real breakthrough in medicine made in Canada was made in 1921 with the discovery of insulin.
This debate is winding down. What is left to say? It has all been said. I listened to the Hon. Member of the Liberal Party who just spoke actually twist things. I do not say that he was deliberately misleading the House because I do not think he understands. We need research and development in Canada.
At the present time, the ratio of research and development to sales in the pharmaceutical industry is 4.7 per cent. We have been guaranteed by the Bill that by 1990, that ratio will be 8 per cent and by 1995, it will be 10 per cent. The sales of pharmaceuticals presently amount to $2.5 billion to $3 billion. Perhaps by 1995, those sales will have grown, but that is already a great amount of money.
The scientific community has responded. It has said that we are right, Canada cannot survive without research and development. Nordic Laboratories in Montreal have committed $35 million to research and development. Universities and hospitals in Calgary and Edmonton have committed $132.9 million. Universities and hospitals in British Columbia have committed $81.6 million. Astra Pharmaceuticals in my own riding of Mississauga has pledged to spend on research and development. These companies have pledged that they will spend $850 million in research and development over the next 10 years. This means that 3,000 new jobs will be created for university-trained research people. The brain-drain to the United States will stop.

May 6, 1987
Patent Act
It is absolutely ludicrous that we should protect intellectual property for only four years. A company in my riding, Smith Kline & French, developed a drug to deal with peptic ulcers. That drug saved $135 million in surgery costs. Imagine the savings that drug made to medical costs in Ontario.
The scientific community has responded. Michel Bergeron, Director of the Department of Physiology at the University of Montreal, and others have said:
We are in full support of the amendments that are in front of the House'to support pharmaceutical discoveries.
A professor in the Faculty of Pharmaceutical Science at the University of British Columbia has said:
You can't have good quality medical care if you don't have good research in the country. These things are tied together.
The Chairman of the Department of Pharmacology at the University of Toronto has said:
Many critics overlook the fact that the $3 billion in research to be spent by Canada's pharmaceutical industry will lead to new and improved treatments, eliminating or reducing the need for surgery and hospitalization.
The scientific community supports this Bill. Most members of the Liberal Party who think support it as well.
Now members of the New Democratic Party have decided to launch a fund-raising campaign, the Hon. Member for Oshawa's (Mr. Broadbent) campaign for fair drug prices. I do not know, Mr. Speaker, if you received one of those little cards, but some of the people on my executive in Mississauga received them. They asked me if it could be true that this man wants them to send money so that he could support the downfall of the pharmaceutical industry, and they laughed at him. Believe me, the campaign did not take off the way he thought it would.
I received a copy of a letter that was sent to the Hon. Member for Oshawa by a constituent of mine. I know my constituent would not mind if I quoted from this letter. It was sent to many places including The Toronto Star, The Globe and Mail, and the Consumers' Association. My constituent had this to say to the Hon. Member for Oshawa:
How dare you misrepresent the drug prices issue to Canadians? As a pharmacologist who understands how new drugs are researched and developed, I am outraged that you should effectively lie to Canadians by omitting any mention in your recent unsolicited letter of the cost and value of drug research for the health of Canadians.
Although basic medical research is also done in universities, it is the "multinational" research-based pharmaceutical companies who spend the money to research, develop and introduce new drug treatments of disease for the sick and needy of ail nationalities.
If the costs of new drug development cannot be recovered by the innovative pharmaceutical industry before their profits are siphoned off by copy-cats with no research overheads, then obviously, new drug development becomes uneconomic and will be phased out.
Who will suffer then, Ed Broadbent? Those with cancer, AIDS, muscular dystrophy, multiple sclerosis, Alzheimer's disease, autoimmune diseases, viral and parasitic diseases, severe skin diseases, etc., in fact, those whose conditions would have been treatable if research had remained a valued and economically feasible human endeavour. The situation you would have us support denies drug developers the right to expect to recover their investments of $100 million and ten years of research for each new medicine they introduce.
Canadians support the concept of improvements in health care, as demonstrated by their generosity in giving to the Cancer Society, Muscular Dystrophy Association, Heart Foundation, etc. University researchers are beneficiaries of these donations, but only Ed Broadbent stands to benefit from the diversion of discretionary money to the "Fund for Fair Drug Prices". Canadians stand to lose out in the long run, both in a financial and in a humane sense, because the development of new drug treatments promises the most economical (and sometimes the only) means of treating these difficult diseases.
I am tired of "positions" and half-fact/half-fiction masquerading as truth when presented to the Canadian public. The truth is not a matter of opinion, but of established facts. When facts are omitted from discussion in order to make opinions more tenable, then the New Democratic Party perpetrates a dastardly and callous lie upon the public.
I want you to listen to this, Mr. Speaker:
I have voted NDP in the past. 1 guarantee it won't happen again,-
Praise the Lord, someone has seen the light. He said that only because any Party that takes the position on the Patent Act adopted by the NDP is fundamentally opposed to research and development in health care and to all that has motivated this man in his 22 years of study of drug treatment of disease.
We have put in place a Drug Prices Review Board chaired by Dr. Harry Eastman. He is a respected gentleman and has guaranteed a lot of safeguards to ensure there will be no increase in drug prices.
Does the board have any teeth? I can tell you it does. It will have the authority to review all prescription drug prices so as to ensure that those prices are fair after taking into account the Consumer Price Index, the price of that drug in other countries, the direct production and marketing cost of the drug, along with any other factor the board considers relevant. If the board finds the price of a particular drug excessive it can set a price ceiling thereby lowering the price. If a company persists in selling above that price ceiling then the board can order its period of patent protection to be revoked, not just on the product in question but on all of its patented drugs. The board has a very strong case to put before the Canadian public.
We must also remember that for the first time there is a federal agency, and I mentioned this before, with provincial participation which can review the 93 per cent of drug prices not subject to generic competition. Up until now they have not been subject to any kind of downward price pressure.
This is a good Bill. It does a lot of things. It will bring in new research and development. Three thousand new jobs will be created in Canada over the next 10 years. About $850 million in new research and plant expansion projects have already been announced. Of the 3,000 new jobs, over half will be for university-trained people. We are going to end the brain drain. We will have increased innovation.
This Bill will improve the quality of Canadian health care, which is very important. More drug research in Canada will result in new and improved treatments for medical problems
May 6, 1987

and better over-all health care. Some new drugs eliminate the need for hospitalization, and I mentioned the drug produced by Smith Kline French in my riding. Surgery as well as harmful side effects will be reduced and consumers will not only benefit from the earlier introduction of drugs into Canada but there will also be the further saving from reduced hospitalization.
We will also get strengthened generic competition. I honestly believe that the generics are not going to suffer from this situation. We know that when drugs are introduced on the market in Canada the generic companies do not rush to copy every one. As a matter of fact, over the past seven years, of 145 drugs introduced in Canada, one was copied. Application has been made to introduce 41 new drugs on the market. Forty will be brought on in the next four years and one in the next five years. These drugs will assist in fighting disease. We look forward to those generic drugs coming on the market. In the past it has taken 9.9 years for a drug to come on the market. Why should the manufacturer not have 10 years' patent protection?
Aside from strengthened generic competition we will have stronger consumer protection, and that is very important. Bill C-22 does that by ensuring that all drug prices are reviewed. That is all drug prices, not only those for which there is generic competition. If this new policy had been in effect since 1969 it could have saved consumers between $226 million and $366 million by 1983. Those savings would have resulted from both the impact of modified compulsory licensing and the effect of the review board in moderating prices. Those savings compare more than favourably with the $211 million in savings estimated by Dr. Eastman in his report. Moreover, the estimated savings under the existing system do not reflect the addition of $70 million in research funds which would have been invested under Bill C-22.
The opposition Parties are going to have to learn sooner or later that they are here to oppose bad legislation, and rightly so. 1 respect them for that. If bad legislation is brought in I will assist them in opposing it. However, I will never assist them in opposing good legislation just for the want of opposing something. The NDP and the Liberals have found that their campaign has fizzled. I mean fizzled. People in Canada are ready to give pharmaceutical companies the rights they deserve in order to manufacture drugs and protect Canadian lives. I urge everyone to stand with me half an hour from now and support Bill C-22.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Questions and comments? Debate.
Mr. Speaker, I was rather interested in the speech by the Hon. Member.
You should be, he knows what he is talking about.
I am not sure about that.

I think he does.
Patent Act
The Canadian people will make that judgment come the next election.
They sure will.

I can tell all those Tories who want to say a few words while I am speaking that even under the most generous conditions, even under the most optimistic projections, at least 100 of them are not coming back here after the next election.
Do you want to make a small wager on that?
I am being extremely charitable in making that prediction.
You are going to eat those words, Neil.

At a very minimum, 100 Tories are not coming back. I want them to think about that when they are leaping up and down supporting measures which are clearly seen by the Canadian public as not being in their best interest.
In the few remarks I want to make about Bill C-22 I think it is worth examining how that Bill came before this House for debate. It came about in a very unusual way. Numerous studies have been done over the past number of years since 1969, and prior thereto, into the pharmaceutical industry in Canada and indeed in other countries around the world. The latest study that was completed by the now famous Dr. Eastman was recognized as the most exhaustive study that has ever been completed not only on the pharmaceutical industry in Canada but elsewhere. Dr. Eastman concluded in his report that Canada's policy that was adopted in 1969 to amend the Patent Act as far as pharmaceutical products are concerned had been a good policy for Canada and certainly for Canadians. He estimated that in 1983 alone Canadian consumers saved $211 million on drug prices as a result of the present policy, which the Government now wants to change.
I think we all must recognize why Professor Eastman was asked to examine Canada's policy and, indeed, why seven commissions prior to Doctor Eastman's inquiry were formed to look into the pharmaceutical industry. Anyone who wants to be open-minded and look at history will discover that Canada has this present policy because prior to 1969 Canadians were paying among the highest drug prices in the world. Governments commissioned these studies to discover why Canada, of all countries, was paying the highest prices in the world for pharmaceutical products.
Those studies came to certain conclusions. The first was that the pharmaceutical industry, which was primarily controlled by multinational corporations, enjoyed a monopoly in price setting on drug products. All of those studies concluded that the only real answer was to remove patent protection and eliminate that monopoly practice from pharmaceutical products, and inject some kind of competition into that industry. Therefore, they recommended to Governments that

May 6, 1987
Patent Act
patent protection be removed and that some compensation should be paid to the pharmaceutical corporations for their cost of research and development.
The conclusion of all those studies was that the pharmaceutical industries had spent a maximum of 4 per cent of total sales on research and development and therefore, if a generic company wished to copy a brand name product it would be required to compensate the multinational corporation with a 4 per cent royalty for making use of that product.
When government Members describe Canadian generic drug manufacturers as a bunch of thieves, as was suggested by one government Member, they should also be honest and point out that those multinationals are being adequately compensated for the use of their product.
All of those commissions concluded that Canada's present policy is a good one for Canada and Canadians. In fact, the House will be interested to know that nearly every other country in the western world has looked at Canada's present policy and found it to be extremely attractive from the point of view of allowing their consumers to reap an equal benefit to those that Canadians now enjoy. Furthermore, during the U.S. Senate hearings in the last several weeks, I believe, a number of witnesses from the United States appeared before that committee and made the very argument that the United States Government should copy Canada's policy for the benefit of U.S. consumers.
I suspect that Canada is changing this policy not because of any pressure from within but primarily because of external pressures placed upon the Canadian Government. In fact, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) admitted as much already, and blamed his European counterparts for placing that pressure on Canada to amend the Patent Act. There is, however, increasing evidence that the pressure is primarily coming from the United States Government, through U.S.-based pharmaceutical corporations, in the free trade negotiations that are currently taking place between the United States and Canadian Governments.
There is ample evidence to indicate that the purpose of changing our policy is not to benefit Canadians but to benefit primarily U.S.-based multinational pharmaceutical manufacturers. I also suspect that a similar reason that pressure is being applied in Canada is that the multinationals recognize that Canada's policy is attractive to other countries and have decided to put the fight on in Canada before these other countries attempt to adopt our policy.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has compared a drug product to that of a widget, or the author of a book. He asks: "How would you like to invent or produce a widget and find someone the next day copying that widget, producing it under another name, and reaping the benefits from that invention?" I reject that absolutely. First, we know that it cannot possibly happen because copyright laws are quite different from Canada's patent policy.
Second, I totally reject the argument that we can compare health products to widgets. A person who requires medication does not have a choice of medication because the doctor makes that decision.
I also argue that pharmaceutical products and their affordability are an integral part of our health care system. We cannot compare people's health and their ability to receive affordable medication with that of manufacturing a widget, as the Minister likes to argue.
The Government makes another argument which is not too convincing but helps to confuse the debate. It suggests that the NDP should not be so concerned because if this policy is adopted it will not increase prices. However, when the Government introduced this legislation it also stated that it would compensate provincial Governments by some $100 million a year for the next four years for any increase in drug costs that they may have to carry under the various drug plans they have for senior citizens, those on welfare and those who cannot afford to purchase their own medication. If this legislation will not result in increased costs, why does the Government propose to provide the provinces to the tune of $400 million over the next four years to compensate for additional costs? That defies logic.
The fact is that this legislation will increase costs. Why do the multinationals want that kind of freedom in the marketplace if it is not to increase profits? If it is to increase profits, we can be sure that the cost of pharmaceutical products in this country will increase as well.
The other part of the argument the Minister makes is that drug prices will not increase, but if they do increase, Canadian taxpayers should not be too concerned because seniors are covered under most provincial drug plans and the disabled receive assistance under the drug plans as well as, in many cases, single-parent families. Where does the Minister think those Governments receive the funds from? They receive the money through taxes. Someone pays the provincial and federal Governments. They do not go to the bank and say: "Give me a chunk of money". Taxpayers will pay for these increased costs if, indeed, provincial Governments decide that this is the way to go to cover the additional cost to their Treasuries. A number of Governments have already sharpened their pencils. They have come to the same conclusion as we have that there certainly will be higher drug costs in the future.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Crystal ball gazing.

No, I do not think it is crystal ball gazing because the Minister himself has said that it will cost $400 million over the next four years to provincial Treasuries, and that is why he is proposing to transfer $400 million in additional compensation to the provinces to cover those increased drug costs. The Government has recognized the possibility of drug price increases, and that is why it proposed this additional compensation to the provinces. The provinces have also
May 6, 1987

sharpened their pencils because the $400 million will not be nearly sufficient to cover their additional costs.
What are the provincial Governments going to do? They receive their revenues from the same place as the federal Government, and that is, from the taxpayers. They are going to have to take a look at their drug plans, and those provinces which provide free drug coverage, such as Ontario, will have to decide whether they can continue with those programs. If it is decided to continue with the programs, how are they going to be funded? Will the provinces go back to the taxpayers and increase provincial taxes? If they decide that this would not be a politically astute thing to do, they may decide, since it has become too costly, to charge a deductible for that program. In other words seniors or disabled individuals may have to pay the first $100, $200, $300, $400 or $500 of drug costs before the provincial plan kicks in. The provinces may decide, rather than impose a deductible, to cut back on the program in some other way. The provincial Governments will not have any choice. They will have to come up with the funds for those plans which are fully paid for.
If the provinces do not want to go in either of those two directions, they could take a look at other social programs they provide and cut back on those in order to cover the drug plans. One way or another, provincial taxpayers are going to pay through the nose as a result of Bill C-22.
The previous speaker said the New Democratic Party has been distorting the facts during this debate. He said that somehow or other the New Democratic Party is the villain in this piece rather than the Government. I have a great deal of respect for some of my friends opposite and I am sure they recognize, as I do, that in the heat of debate very often some Members-not all of them, certainly not the Members in the House at the present time-become strangers to the truth. However, just to satisfy those people who may be listening to this debate that indeed the New Democratic Party has not been distorting the facts, I thought I would indicate what a whole number of obviously knowledgeable people across the country are saying about the Government's proposed legislation.
Hon. Members will not be surprised to learn that the Toronto Star consistently opposes what the Government has been doing primarily based on the arguments we have been presenting. One of the headlines of an article on February 19 of this year reads: "Why the drug patent legislation is all wrong". The article goes on to give a very detailed analysis of the legislation and points out quite clearly why this legislation should not be supported either by Members of this House or by the Canadian public.
The Financial Post, which one could hardly call a socialist newspaper, on December 15, 1986, carried a headline which read: "Catch-22 triples in Tory drug Bill".
1 will not quote the whole article but it makes a couple of points in refuting the arguments of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. The article reads, and I quote:
Business of the House
First, the Minister argues that giving firms the exclusive right to market new drugs for 10 years won't raise the prices of such drugs. But the reason you want the patent in the first place is to give the firm a monopoly so it can charge a monopoly price and make what may look like a monopoly profit, but is really (at least in part) a return to its R and D investment. If prices aren't going to rise, the patent has no value. So why give it?
That is the first Catch-22. The article goes on to say, and I quote:
Then the Minister argues that under the current system of compulsory licensing, generic firms take 10 years on average to bring their copies of new pharmaceuticals on to the market. But if inventors already have 10 years of effective protection, why do we need a system of 10 year patents?
It terms this as "Catch-44". The articles continues:
Finally, the Government wants to establish a drug prices review board to ensure that abuses do not take place. But if we want monopoly prices in the first 10 years after a drug's invention (so invention will be encouraged), and if competition from the generics will be available after that, why do we need such a board?
And it terms that "Catch-66". My time has almost expired but I could quote The Globe and Mail whose headline reads: "Patent change may not mean better drugs". I could quote nearly every editorial from any newspaper across this country which has come out in opposition to what the Government is proposing in this legislation.
In conclusion, may I say that while I have heard speakers from the government side urge Members of the House to support this legislation when it comes to its final vote tonight at six o'clock, I will make the opposite plea. If those 100 Tories about whom I spoke about earlier, who are facing certain defeat in the next election, want to save their hides, they should vote against this legislation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask my hon. friend a couple of questions with respect to the campaign for
fair drug prices, a campaign of the New Democratic Party which went out across almost all of the land. Lirst, I want to comment on a three-page letter signed by the Leader of the New Democratic Party which does not mention one word with respect to research and the importance of it or even the lack of research in Canada.
The New Democratic Party is always talking about honesty and openness and how frank it is with the Canadian people. Could the Hon. Member answer these questions? How much money has been raised on this campaign? How much money was spent to promote the campaign? What has the New Democratic Party done with the money that it raised? Has it gone to promote just the New Democratic Party? How is this money to be spent? Even better, will the New Democratic Party table the books with respect to this campaign which will show how well it did in raising this money?

Mr. Speaker, I find myself in the same difficulty, I suppose, that some cabinet Ministers find themselves in when they are asked questions on how their Party formulates things or how their caucus does things. Quite frankly, I do not have answers to these questions because I was not involved in that part of the campaign. As the Hon. Member knows, my role in our fight against this legislation was to go out into the country to meet with senior citizens' groups, with members of disabled organizations and disabled people. I went to the Atlantic provinces, for example, and had an excellent meeting with all types of service organizations-
And misled them!

I had an excellent reception in Edmonton, Alberta, and in Saskatchewan and Manitoba-all over the place. 1 realize that the Hon. Member asks me these questions honestly and that he expects frank answers. All I can suggest to him is that I do not have the information about which he asks, but I would be pleased to try to find it out for him and to provide it to him. I am sure he would be quite interested, as I would, with respect to how effective the campaign was.

Mr. Speaker, I heard the Hon. Member from Mississauga interject the comment that when my friend, the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young), was travelling across the country and talking to groups he misled them. I note that the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops and organizations such as the Consumers' Association of Canada opposed this Bill when it was first introduced and have opposed it since. Will the Hon. Member for Beaches tell us whether he believes that we are so efficient and so effective that we could mislead the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops and organizations such as the Consumers' Association of Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I have absolutely no hesitation in assuring you and the House that, first, it was neither the Official Opposition nor the New Democratic Party which took off in opposition to this legislation. Senior citizens' organizations in the country were way ahead of the political Parties in terms of expressing their opposition to this legislation. It was
May 6, 1987

they who asked me to sit down with them last July. I will tell Hon. Members that I met with them downstairs in this very same building at their request. As a result of meeting with senior citizens' groups, consumer groups, the National Action Committee on the Status of Women and others the real concern was first raised with us. It was we in our role as an opposition Party who lent assistance to their fight against this legislation.
I have no hesitation in saying that I am quite proud of the role this Party has taken and the lead given to opposing this legislation in the House of Commons. I only wish that we had another six months in which to continue our opposition. Unfortunately, the Government decided to close off debate on this legislation and we are now faced with a vote in about nine more minutes, something which I consider to be quite unfortunate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, throughout the debate on this legislation, the Hon. Member has accused the Government of taking sides with the multinationals. I want to ask the Hon. Member what he thinks of the comments made in the course of this debate by eminent persons across Canada, and I would like to name a few from Quebec, because they are more familiar to me. For instance, Dr. Michel Chretien, Director of the Montreal Clinical Research Institute, Dr. Yves Morin, the famous cardiologist, Mr. Jacques Gagne of the University of Montreal, and all the people who appeared before the Committee, begging the Government to expedite the legislation because no more research was being done in Quebec and all the young scientists and academics were going to the United States or elsewhere. How does he reconcile his position with that of the people I just mentioned, whose purpose in life is not to make money but to improve the health of their fellow citizens?

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to answer that because I also met with those individuals. I do not mind telling you exactly what I told them. I could understand their desire to accept any money that they could find for research because of the way in which the Government had cut back on the amount of moneys targeted for research across the country. By the way, those people were a minority. A large percentage of the people in research fields and universities recognize exactly what the Government is doing and certainly do not support it.
I told them that if they think the answers to their problems in research and development are to be found in this legislation, they are being extremely naive, even though I understand why they could be attracted to the position which they finally took. On close examination of the press releases put out by drug companies promising all kinds of additional expenditures for research and development, if this legislation is passed, you will find that they were not talking about additional moneys for research and development but for clinical research. Anyone
Patent Act
who has even a shallow understanding of the field knows there is a vast difference between clinical research and research and development.

Mr. Speaker, I see that it is shortly after six o'clock and I do not have much time for debate. This debate has gone on for quite some time. I heard the Member for Beaches (Mr. Young) saying that debate had been closed off. This legislation had 82 hours of consideration in committee before which 46 groups or 120 individuals appeared. One hundred and forty written briefs were received, and by the time I finish speaking there will have been 28 hours of debate in the House. I think that probably all of the salient points will have been touched upon by that time. By this time literally hundreds of points have probably been regurgitated too many times.
I am interested in speaking on this subject because I come from the City of Saskatoon which is unlike the Cities of Montreal and Toronto where the bulk of this research will probably take place. However, Saskatoon has a major university, a major private sector in research and development, and a number of federal and provincial government laboratories. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that people in the university community are very interested in, perhaps for the first time in their lives, working somewhere in Canada at least, if not in western Canada, in research after having received a graduate degree from the university in Saskatoon.
I took the time to meet with the faculty and graduate students at the College of Pharmacy of the University of Saskatchewan about six weeks ago. They were elated that there would be a chance to do something right here in Canada with regard to research. Believe it or not, there are already two companies which are potentially interested in locating in little old Saskatoon which has a population of 180,000, if this legislation passes. That is why I am interested in this legislation.
We all remember a lady by the name of Judy Erola who was in this House in the previous administration. She was the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and commissioned Professor Harry Eastman to do a study on the pharmaceutical industry. I read with interest a letter that Judy Erola wrote to the Winnipeg Free Press on April 22. She said: "I believe that many people have fundamentally misinterpreted this Bill".
I appreciate that it is the job of the Opposition to oppose certain pieces of legislation. However, when incorrect or slanted information is going to the public and is picked up by the media, it does not take very long to be misinterpreted right across the country. I believe that is precisely the reason so many people are scared to death of this legislation. They are only looking at the nickels and dimes rather than at the benefits. They are not considering the Drug Prices Review Board which will review 100 per cent of the drugs in the country for the first time in the history of Canada. That is what this legislation is all about. It is not only about research

May 6, 1987
Patent Act
and development, although I think that is very important. We must think about consumers.
A poll was done by Decima Research for the pharmaceutical industry. Twelve hundred people were polled between February 26 and March 4, 1987. The results show that 65 per cent of the people in Canada thought this legislation was good after hearing the main arguments for and against it. It is also interesting to note that 82 per cent of the people polled would support the Bill if the Government ensured that drug price increases would be no greater than the increase in the rate of inflation.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the Drug Prices Review Board will report to Parliament annually. There will be a policy review every four years and a parliamentary review after 10 years. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there is consumer protection built into this legislation.
I would like to conclude by saying that I appreciated having these eight minutes to speak on this very important piece of legislation. As the former Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, Judy Erola, said, if you think about it, Bill C-22 is better protection for all Canadians.
